newsitem.title: UK: Britain reacts sharply to Toyota remarks.
newsitem.headline: Britain reacts sharply to Toyota remarks.

text.p: Britain reacted sharply on Wednesday after Japanese carmaker Toyota appeared to rule out building new factories in Britain and said investment could shift to Europe if London stays out of Europe's single currency.
Toyota President Hiroshi Okuda said the Japanese carmaker was already reviewing its levels of investment in Britain.
"Regardless of whether Britain joins (the EMU), I have a feeling that it would be excessive if we made additional (investments) in Britain," Okuda told reporters in Tokyo.
But he said Toyota would shift its European investments to continental Europe if Britain did not join economic and monetary union (EMU), due to be launched in 1999.
The ruling Conservative government says that if it wins the next general election, due to be held by the end of May, it is very unlikely to take Britain into the first stage of EMU.

A spokesman for Prime Minister John Major said he was not prepared to take Okuda's remarks at face value, saying Toyota only last year announced 200 million pounds ($325 million) in additional investment at its plant in Derbyshire, central England.
"That indicates to me great confidence in the United Kingdom," he said. "The UK is the place to be and remains so."
Trade Secretary Ian Lang said the government had always stood up for Japanese carmakers based in Britain.

"The British government consistently backed the Japanese car industry in the single market to ensure that Japanese cars built in the United Kingdom have no restrictions placed on them within the European Union," he said.

In a statement aimed at reassuring Japanese businessmen, he added: "No decision on economic and monetary union has been taken. We have made it quite clear that we will not make this decision until we know all the facts."
But his remarks appeared at odds with the Toyota chairman's, who was asked in Tokyo if Toyota's investment in Britain would fall if London decided to opt out of EMU.

"Rather than decreasing the amount, we will leave investments as they are now. But if we were to make fresh investments, we would prefer to make them in continental Europe rather than Britain," said Okuda, Toyota's top executive.
Toyota last year built 117,000 cars at its plant in Derbyshire, central England.
Conservative Party officials were clearly irritated at the remarks, which came hours after Lang had trumpeted Britain's success in winning inward investment.

Major, trying to drive home the message that his government is good for business, was visiting South Wales, where the Korean giant LG Group announced a 1.7 billion pound investment to build two electronic plants.
But Edwina Currie, the Conservative member of parliament and former minister whose Derbyshire South constituency includes the Toyota factory, said she was not surprised at the warning.

"Toyota have been twitching for months. They wrote to me in December and said that they strongly believe it is essential for the United Kingdom to remain as an integral part of the European Union," she told BBC radio.

"If we are going to be a sort of fringe nation, a sort of follow-on country, then all these big Asian countries are not going to be terribly interested," said Currie, a fierce foe of Conservative Eurosceptics who want looser links with Europe.
The opposition Labour Party, which enjoys a wide opinion poll lead, seized on the remarks.

Economics spokesman Gordon Brown said: "This is the first sign of industry reacting to the Tories' (Conservatives') infighting and disunity over Europe. The Tories are now putting British jobs at risk and 3.5 million jobs depend on Europe." ($1=.6175 Pound)
